name: Maya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Maya, 43, and I operate a roof bolter at a large underground mine. I set the machine under the marked ground, check the bolts, and write down any roof movement before the next crew comes in. I've got a vocational certificate and several years underground; I'm competent but earn toward the lower end of this job. My partner delivers parcels on a contract, and we have two school-age children, a mortgage and less than a month of savings. I use AI now and then to explain a manual term, but only after another operator has tried a tool would I bring it into my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little form filling help sounds useful if roof checks stay with the crew. The mine should spend any saved minutes on better inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bolter work looks steady here, but the parcel contract can have weak weeks. A single mortgage payment would take most of our savings right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my roof bolter checks and hand the next crew a clear shift record. I'd compare three months of parcel income with our fixed bills this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the bills already, even if AI never becomes much more than a form helper. My partner's delivery route lost two days last month, and we had to delay a school purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which school purchase waited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our younger child needed new sports shoes, and we waited until the next delivery payment came through. It was a small thing, but it showed how little room the budget has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust automated roof notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read them if they came with the measurements and the person who checked them. I wouldn't sign a roof record I hadn't compared with what I saw from the bolter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew planning software could alter where we bolt before robots enter the tunnel. We need to see ground measurements alongside any computer instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands still run the bolter, but fewer survey staff might leave us with weaker explanations. If targets go up, I could lose the overtime that closes our monthly gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the survey lead to demonstrate the ground map tool after it has worked on another heading. I'd keep copies of roof measurements when new targets change the sequence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because I can't afford a shift trimmed by a faster plan. I will use a tool once the survey lead can show where its information came from, but a map is not the roof above my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a wrong map?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the machine and call the survey lead before setting another bolt. Once a marker was off by a metre after a wet week; we measured again rather than guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the union to intervene?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine ignored the measurements, yes. First I'd bring the record to the supervisor and ask for the sequence to be corrected.

fieldNote: She expects **thinking AI** to alter survey and planning before it replaces the hands-on bolter operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for separate 2028 planning and 2031 robot schedules from the mine. The workers need paid transition time before a bolter can run itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, AI could do survey plans while I still set bolts. At 48 in 2031, a capable robot could take my machine and leave few local mines to apply to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the rail maintenance depot about track inspection vacancies this year. I'd cut the monthly streaming bundles now and build one month's emergency reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed because I expect my bolter hours to go when the robots arrive, and the house payment is already hard. I lie awake thinking about a gap between the last mine wage and the first wage elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the rail depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The depot is near the children's school, and track inspection uses careful measurements. I don't know if robots will take that work too; I want to hear their hiring plans before paying for another certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Dev that we need the extra subscriptions gone and a list of nearby employers. I wouldn't tell the children the mine is closing, because that isn't what the card says.

The workers need **paid transition time** before a bolter can run itself.

feel: **Alarmed** by expected bolter loss and sleepless wage worries.
S2.quote: I lie awake thinking about a gap between the last mine wage and the first wage elsewhere.
fieldNote: She expects **2031 robot bolters** to threaten her main wage while the household holds less than one month's expenses.
She explores a nearby **rail depot** and removes small subscriptions without pretending track work is permanently safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to publish a 2034 bolter plan while families can still change course. Paid training should follow actual vacancies, not just a glossy course list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AI could draw roof plans while I still work the machine. At 51 in 2034, our children will be older but the mortgage will still need a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd visit the rail depot this spring to ask which inspection certificate it accepts. I'd apply for a funded track inspection course if the depot confirms it leads to paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the household today, though five years before the thinking change lets me ask better questions. I could take a course once the depot confirms the jobs, but I won't borrow money on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the written entry requirements and the pay scale, then compare them with our mortgage. A certificate that leads only to casual days would leave us where we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep working at the mine meanwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd keep the bolter shifts until another employer offers paid work. We can't live on the courier contract while I study full-time.

feel: **Anxious** now, with time to verify another route.
S3.quote: A certificate that leads only to casual days would leave us where we are.

She protects current **bolter wages** and tests course value against written entry rules, pay and the household mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2039 robots leave time for a measured change, if the mine gives real dates. The crew deserves a written machine plan for each heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, AI might write roof plans while I still install bolts. At 56 in 2039, I may still need a full wage after the children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the bolter shifts and review our mortgage balance every six months. I'd ask the rail depot next year about inspection jobs before buying a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about our cash this year, but the later robot date gives me time to test a second route. I won't call 56 retirement when we haven't even built a month's reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a good run of paid shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the extra pay into the reserve until it covers a mortgage month. Then we'd have a little room to pay for the course if the depot says it is required.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an actual offer covered the move and the children's school change. There are few nearby mines, and another bolter seat might face the same robot timetable.

fieldNote: Her **current cash shortage** keeps the long scenario tense even while a 2039 robot arrival gives planning time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because 2031 robots could take my bolter shifts while the children are still in school and our savings are tiny. A written machine schedule, funded training tied to real jobs and help with a wage gap would matter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the next job offers regular hours. A new badge is no use if it pays only for two days when the mortgage needs a full month.

headlineQuote: A new badge is no use if it pays only for two days when the mortgage needs a full month.
portrait: Maya is a **43-year-old** experienced roof bolter operator with a vocational certificate and lower mine pay.
Her partner's parcel contract varies; two school-age children, a **mortgage** and thin savings make steady hours essential.
She tries **AI occasionally** and accepts tools after a trusted colleague shows how they perform on real ground.
A fast robot arrival **alarms** her; longer warnings let her verify depot jobs, course value and wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 robots could remove bolter shifts before the household builds reserves.
whatWouldHelp: A **written machine schedule**, funded training tied to paid jobs and help through a wage gap would protect the mortgage.
